title: The Human Body · Episode 4
chapters: Your skin: the organ you wear

units.t: The Human Body. Episode four.
In this episode: Your skin: the organ you wear, How a cut heals, How your senses work and The human brain.
Part one. Your skin: the organ you wear.
It is waterproof, self-repairing, temperature-controlled and covered in sensors, and you are wearing it right now.
Meet the most underrated organ you have.
The organ you wear.
Lay an adult's skin flat and it would cover roughly two square metres, and weigh several kilograms.
It is the body's largest organ.
It keeps water in and germs out, shields you from sunlight, helps control temperature, makes vitamin D and heals itself after cuts.
It is also a sensor.
Specialised nerve endings respond to light touch, vibration, pressure, stretching, heat, cold and damage.
They are not spread evenly.
Fingertips, lips and tongue are packed with receptors, while your back has far fewer, which is why it is hard to tell whether one or two pencil points are pressing on it.
Fingerprint ridges form before birth and help with grip and fine texture.
Even identical twins have different fingerprints, because small variations in the womb shape the ridges.
Layers that renew.
Skin has three layers.
The epidermis is thin, but it faces the world.
Its top is flattened dead cells packed with tough keratin, forming a waterproof, germ-resistant barrier.
Beneath it, the dermis is woven from collagen and elastin fibres that give strength and stretch, and holds blood vessels, nerve endings, hair roots and sweat glands.
The fat layer below cushions you, stores energy and holds in heat.
At the base of the epidermis, cells divide constantly and are pushed upwards, filling with keratin and dying on the way.
The journey takes roughly a month, so you grow a new outer skin many times a year.
A popular claim says most household dust is dead skin, but much indoor dust comes from outside.
The colour of skin.
Cells called melanocytes at the bottom of the epidermis make a pigment called melanin.
People of all skin tones have broadly similar numbers of melanocytes.
What differs is how much melanin they make and what type.
More melanin, especially the darker form, gives deeper skin tones and stronger natural protection against ultraviolet radiation.
When skin is exposed to the sun, melanocytes ramp up production.
That is a tan: a sign skin has been damaged and is trying to defend itself.

Scientists think skin colour varies so much because our ancestors lived under very different levels of sunlight, balancing protection from UV against the need to make vitamin D. In a high-UV country like Australia, sun protection matters for everyone.
Cooling and goosebumps.
On a hot Brisbane afternoon, your skin becomes a cooling system.
Millions of sweat glands release watery sweat, and as it evaporates it carries heat away.
Blood vessels near the surface widen, so warm blood sends heat out, which is why your face flushes.
In the cold the reverse happens: vessels narrow to keep warmth near your core.
A second type of sweat gland, found mainly in the armpits and groin, releases a thicker sweat.
It is odourless at first, and the smell comes from skin bacteria breaking it down.
Goosebumps are made by tiny muscles that pull hairs upright.
In furry animals this traps insulating air or makes them look bigger.
In us, it is mostly a curious leftover.
Ageing and sun protection.
As we age, skin makes less collagen and elastin, grows thinner and holds less moisture, which is why wrinkles and sagging appear.
But much of what people think of as ageing skin is actually sun damage.
Compare the skin on someone's forearm with the inner upper arm and the difference can be striking.

Australia has some of the highest rates of skin cancer in the world, so sun protection is the single most useful habit: shade, clothing, a broad-brimmed hat, sunglasses and sunscreen, especially when the UV index is 3 or above.
Getting to know your own skin and checking for new or changing spots is also worthwhile.
This is general information, not medical advice, so for any concern see a doctor or visit healthdirect.
The key idea: Skin is your largest organ, covering about two square metres and packed with touch sensors, especially in the fingertips.
Part two. How a cut heals.
Slice your finger and your body launches a carefully timed rescue operation, from emergency plugging to months of quiet rebuilding.
Stopping the leak.
The moment skin is cut, damaged blood vessels tighten to reduce blood flow.
Tiny cell fragments called platelets touch the exposed tissue and become sticky.
They clump into a soft plug and release chemicals that call in more platelets.
At the same time a chain of clotting proteins switches on, step by step, until fibrinogen is converted into long strands of fibrin.
These strands weave through the plug like a net, trapping red cells and turning liquid blood into a solid clot.
As the surface dries out, it becomes the familiar crusty scab.
The clean-up crew.
Around two thousand years ago the Roman writer Celsus described the four classic signs of inflammation: redness, heat, swelling and pain.
They do not mean something is going wrong.
Damaged cells release chemical alarms that widen nearby blood vessels, bringing extra blood that makes the area red and warm.
Leakier vessel walls let fluid and immune cells seep into the tissue, causing swelling.
Within hours, white blood cells called neutrophils arrive to kill bacteria.
Macrophages follow, large cells that swallow debris, dead cells and germs.
They also signal the next wave of repair cells to start work, which makes them the managers of healing.
Rebuilding the tissue.
After a few days the wound enters its building phase.
Cells called fibroblasts move in and make collagen, the tough protein that gives skin its strength.
New capillaries sprout to supply oxygen and nutrients.
Together they form granulation tissue, the pink, slightly bumpy surface you may see in a healing graze.
Meanwhile, skin cells at the edges multiply and crawl across the gap, sliding under the scab until they meet in the middle.
Some fibroblasts turn into cells that contract, gently pulling the wound edges closer.
Once the new skin is complete, the scab is no longer needed and falls away.
The long remodel.
The final phase is the slowest.
The first collagen is laid down hastily.
Over following months the body breaks it down and replaces it with stronger, better organised fibres.
A scar that looked red and raised often fades and flattens over a year or more.
Even so, scar tissue never becomes perfect skin.
It typically regains at most around 80 per cent of the original strength, and it usually lacks hair follicles and sweat glands.
Curiously, researchers have found that wounds in early foetuses can heal without any scar at all.
Understanding how is a long-standing goal of wound research.
Care and what slows healing.
Many of us were told to let cuts breathe.
In 1962 British researcher George Winter tested this on pigs, whose skin is similar to ours.
Shallow wounds covered with plastic film healed considerably faster than wounds left in the air.
A dry scab is a barrier that new skin cells must tunnel under, while a moist surface lets them glide across.
So clean small cuts gently and keep them covered.
Healing needs blood supply, oxygen and raw materials.
Smoking narrows blood vessels, diabetes can damage circulation, and collagen needs protein and vitamin C. Healing also slows with age.
Seek medical help for wounds that are deep, gaping, very dirty, caused by animal bites, or showing spreading infection.
For severe bleeding, apply firm pressure and call 000.
The key idea: Within seconds of a cut, blood vessels tighten and platelets and fibrin plug the hole, forming a clot that dries into a scab.
Part three. How your senses work.
You have far more than five senses.
And every one of them is your brain's interpretation, not a direct window on the world.
More than five.
The idea of five senses goes back to Aristotle.
Scientists now count many more, depending on how you define a sense.
Proprioception tells you where your limbs are without looking, which is how you can touch your nose with your eyes closed.
The vestibular system in your inner ear senses balance and motion.
Separate receptors detect temperature and pain.
Interoception reports your internal state, like hunger, thirst, a full bladder or a racing heart.
All of them work the same basic way: specialised receptor cells convert physical signals into nerve impulses that the brain interprets.
How we see.
Light enters through the cornea and lens, which focus it onto the retina at the back of the eye.
The iris adjusts the pupil to control how much light gets in.
The retina holds about 120 million rods, which work in dim light but don't see colour, and about 6 million cones, which detect colour in three types, roughly sensitive to red, green and blue.
Cones are packed into a small central spot, the fovea, which gives your sharpest vision.
The image on the retina is upside down; the brain flips it.
Each eye also has a blind spot where the optic nerve leaves, which your brain fills in.
Hearing and balance.
Sound waves vibrate the eardrum.
Three tiny bones amplify the vibrations and pass them to the cochlea, a fluid-filled spiral about the size of a pea.
Thousands of hair cells bend with the vibrations, different parts responding to different pitches.
Young people typically hear from about 20 to 20,000 vibrations per second, and the upper limit drops with age.
Loud noise can permanently damage hair cells, which don't regrow in humans.
Next to the cochlea, three semicircular canals sense head rotation as fluid lags behind and bends hair cells, and tiny crystals shift with gravity.
When these disagree with vision, as when reading in a car, you may get motion sickness.
Spinning makes you dizzy because the fluid keeps moving.
Smell, taste and touch.
Taste and smell detect molecules.
Taste buds, mostly on the tongue, are replaced every week or two, which is why a burnt tongue recovers.
Humans have around 400 types of smell receptor, and combinations let us tell apart far more odours than once believed.
Smell signals travel almost directly to brain areas for emotion and memory, which is why a scent can instantly bring back a place.
Sudden loss of smell is worth mentioning to a doctor.
Skin has receptors for light touch, pressure, vibration, stretch, heat, cold and pain.
Fingertips and lips are packed with them, so the brain's touch map, the 'homunculus', has huge hands and lips.
Many receptors adapt quickly, so you stop noticing your clothes.
People born unable to feel pain often suffer serious injuries unknowingly.
Brain-built reality.
Your brain combines information from different senses, fills gaps and makes predictions.
In the McGurk effect, watching lips say one sound makes you hear another.
Expectations change taste: the same wine can taste better when people are told it's expensive.
Some people have synaesthesia, such as seeing colours when hearing music.
Perception is an active construction, not a camera recording.
Protect what you have.
Australia's strong sun makes sunglasses and hats worthwhile, as UV contributes to cataracts.
Regular eye tests can catch glaucoma before you notice vision loss.
A common workplace guide treats noise averaging 85 decibels over eight hours as the limit before protection is needed; earbuds at high volume count.
See a doctor promptly about sudden loss of smell, hearing or vision, or new dizziness.
The key idea: Beyond the classic five, we also sense body position, balance, temperature, pain and internal states.
Part four. The human brain.
4-kilogram organ with 86 billion nerve cells, running on about the power of a dim light bulb.
Small, thirsty, efficient.
The adult brain weighs about 1.
3 to 1.
4 kilograms, roughly 2 per cent of your body weight, yet it uses about 20 per cent of your energy, even at rest.
That is around 20 watts, about the power of a dim light bulb, which is remarkably efficient compared with computers doing far less.
It is about 75 per cent water and has the consistency of soft tofu, so it floats in protective fluid inside the skull.
It has no pain receptors of its own, which is why some brain surgery can be done while the patient is awake.
Neurons and synapses.
The brain holds roughly 86 billion nerve cells called neurons, plus a similar number of supporting glial cells.
Neurons send electrical signals along their length.
They then release chemical messengers called neurotransmitters, such as dopamine and serotonin, which cross tiny gaps called synapses to the next cell.
Each neuron can connect with thousands of others, creating an estimated 100 trillion or more connections.
Your thoughts, memories and feelings are patterns of activity across these networks.
Regions and lobes.
The cerebrum is the large, wrinkled outer part.
It handles thinking, language, memory, senses and voluntary movement, and its folds pack more surface area into the skull.
The cerebellum, tucked underneath at the back, fine-tunes balance and learned movements like riding a bike.
The brainstem links the brain to the spinal cord and runs breathing, heart rate, swallowing and sleep cycles.
Each side of the cerebrum has four lobes.
The frontal lobes handle planning, self-control and personality, and are among the last areas to mature, into the twenties.
The parietal lobes process touch and space.
The temporal lobes handle hearing, language and memory, and contain the hippocampus.
The occipital lobes process vision.
Two brain myths.
You may have heard that we use only 10 per cent of our brains.
Scans show activity across nearly every region over a day, even in sleep, and damage almost anywhere causes noticeable problems.
An energy-hungry organ that was 90 per cent idle would make no evolutionary sense.
The myth probably grew from misquoted early psychology and survives through movies and self-help marketing.
A newer myth is that brain-training games sharpen your mind for everyday life.
A major 2016 review found that practice makes people better at the games and very similar tasks, but found little good evidence that the gains carry over to everyday thinking.
That same year, the maker of Lumosity paid US$2 million to settle US Federal Trade Commission charges that its advertising was deceptive.
Learning real skills and staying active are better bets.
Rewiring and care.
Your brain physically changes with experience, a property called neuroplasticity.
Learning strengthens or forms connections between neurons, and the adult brain keeps changing throughout life.
London taxi drivers who spent years memorising about 25,000 streets had a larger rear hippocampus than bus drivers on set routes.
After a stroke, other areas can sometimes take over lost functions with rehabilitation.
Brain health is tied to overall health.
Regular exercise increases blood flow to the brain and is one of the best-supported ways to protect thinking skills with age.
Sleep clears waste and consolidates memories.
Social connection and learning are linked to lower dementia risk.
Managing blood pressure, not smoking and limiting alcohol protect your brain too, and a helmet protects it directly.
The key idea: The brain is about 2 per cent of your body weight but uses about 20 per cent of your energy.
Quick recall. Answer out loud, or just in your head.
Question one. Why is it hard to tell whether one or two pencil points are touching your back?
Answer. The back has far fewer touch receptors.
Question two. How does the body turn liquid blood into a solid clot?
Answer. Protein strands weave a net that traps cells.
Question three. How can you touch your nose with your eyes closed?
Answer. A sense tells you where your limbs are.
Question four. What makes the brain's energy use remarkable?
Answer. It uses about 20 per cent of the body's energy at about 2 per cent of its weight.
That's the end of this episode. The questions are waiting in your review, so you can lock in what you heard.
